$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /8}{(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))}^{2} & ={(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}))}^{2} \\  & ={(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))}^{2} \\  & ={(1+2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2} \\  & ={(1+\sqrt{2})}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot \sqrt{2}+{(\sqrt{2})}^{2} \\  & =1+2\sqrt{2}+2 \\  & =3+2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

Substituting $x=\dfrac{\sqrt \pi}{2}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \sqrt{\pi }/2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2{x}^{2}-\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(2{(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2})}^{2}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(2(\frac{\pi }{4})-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Below are the graphs of the two most important trigonometric functions, $\sin(x)$ and $\cos(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14258704/assets/29be90e6dd4312a97eb2fce107d7bf4d0158e98cb3e52b8df60548807fa2881c.png)

For any *finite* real number $a$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a}\sin x=\sin (a) \qquad\text{and}\qquad\lim_\limits{x\to a}\cos x=\cos (a).
$$

For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1 \\ {lim}_{x\to 2\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})=-0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

However, the limits at infinity do not exist. As $x$ approaches $\infty$ or $-\infty$, the values of $\sin(x)$ and $\cos(x)$ oscillate between $1$ and $−1$ forever. So, we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to \pm \infty} \sin x=\text{DNE}\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lim_\limits{x\to \pm \infty} \cos x=\text{DNE}.
$$

tutorials.name: Limits of Tangent
tutorials.problem:
Below is the graph of the tangent function $y=\tan(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14258704/assets/a1137c40e534ef7536e5f64d1e6d58e7440eb92e8dd8ff99954cb7c9ff8fab2f.png)

Note that $\tan x$ is not defined at the vertical asymptotes $x= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$ where $n$ is an integer. However, everywhere else, the limit of the tangent function is the value of the tangent function:

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to a} \tan (x)=\tan\left(a\right),\qquad a\neq \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi,
$$

For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /6}\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

However, the limits at infinity do not exist. As $x$ approaches $\infty$ or $-\infty,$ the values of $\tan(x)$ keep oscillating, and we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to \pm \infty} \tan x=\text{DNE} .
$$

Note that $\tan x$ is not defined at the vertical asymptotes $x= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$ where $n$ is an integer. However, everywhere else, the limit of the tangent function is the value of the tangent function:

For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /6}\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}

tutorials.name: Limits at the Vertical Asymptotes of Tangent
tutorials.problem:
Let's take another look at the graph of the tangent function $y=\tan(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14258704/assets/a1137c40e534ef7536e5f64d1e6d58e7440eb92e8dd8ff99954cb7c9ff8fab2f.png)

As we can see from the graph, $x = \pm \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pm \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \ldots$ are the points where $y=\tan (x)$ has vertical asymptotes. Both the left and right-sided limits at those points are infinite. In particular,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to \pi/2^{-}}\tan(x)=\infty,\qquad \lim_\limits{x\to \pi/2^{+}}\tan(x)=-\infty.
$$

Since the left and right-sided limits are not equal, we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to \pi/2}\tan(x)=\textrm{DNE}.
$$

In general, at any vertical asymptote $x= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$ where $n$ is an integer, the limit is undefined:

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to \pi/2+n\pi}\tan(x)=\textrm{DNE}.
$$
